memorial_note: Endurance is a protected Antarctic historic site. All 28 crew survived. Observe, photograph and leave the ship undisturbed.

entries.title: Endurance: Shackleton's polar ship
paragraphs: Endurance carried Sir Ernest Shackleton's Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition into the Weddell Sea in 1914-15. Built in 1912 at the Framnæs yard in Sandefjord, Norway, and launched under the name Polaris, she was a three-masted barquentine reinforced for polar ice; Shackleton bought and renamed her in January 1914. Pack ice closed around her in January 1915, and after ten months drifting, beset, the ice finally crushed her hull. Captain Frank Worsley recorded her sinking position on 21 November 1915. All 28 men aboard survived; they camped on the drifting ice and eventually reached Elephant Island, from where Shackleton and five others made the 1,300 km open-boat journey to South Georgia for rescue.

The wreck was found on 5 March 2022 by the Endurance22 expedition, organised by the Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust (FMHT) aboard the South African polar vessel S.A. Agulhas II -- exactly 100 years to the day after Shackleton was buried at Grytviken, South Georgia. She lies 3,008 m deep in the Weddell Sea, within the search area the team had defined before departure. Mensun Bound, the expedition's Director of Exploration, called her "by far the finest wooden shipwreck I have ever seen. It is upright, well proud of the seabed, intact, and in a brilliant state of preservation."

The wreck had already been designated a protected Historic Site and Monument (HSM No. 93) under the Antarctic Treaty System in 2019, three years before anyone knew exactly where she lay. The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), working with Historic England, now leads the Conservation Management Plan for the site.

No dedicated multibeam survey covers this part of the Weddell Sea; the terrain uses GMRT's coarser GEBCO-derived grid, smoothing small features. Endurance22's published photographs and survey report show the 44 m ship in much finer detail.

entries.title: The hull, upright and intact
paragraphs: Endurance rests upright on the seabed, her hull essentially intact -- a rare survival for a wooden ship a century after sinking. Her keel was four layers of solid oak, 2.2 m thick in total, and her planking was oak and Norwegian fir up to 30 in thick, sheathed in greenheart for extra strength against ice: exactly the build that let her hold together against the pack for ten months, and that has kept her hull sound on the seabed since.

The Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust's team, led by Director of Exploration Mensun Bound, surveyed her with Saab Sabertooth hybrid underwater vehicles fitted with Voyis optical laser scanners, capturing about 25,000 high-resolution images that were digitally stitched into a precise 44 m bow-to-stern 3D composite.
The preserved hull stands above the sediment, with deck rails, broken spars and the stern fittings still recognizable.

entries.title: "ENDURANCE", and the star of her old name
paragraphs: The ship's name is still clearly legible on the stern, painted directly below the taffrail. Above it is a five-pointed star -- a survival of her original name, Polaris, the pole star, under which she was launched at the Framnæs yard in 1912 before Shackleton bought and renamed her.
Finding the name intact after 106 years on the seabed was one of the expedition's most striking moments, and it is the clearest piece of evidence that this is, beyond doubt, Shackleton's ship.
The stern scan sits about 20 m from the hull's centre.

facts.value: five-pointed star, from the ship's original name Polaris

entries.title: The wheel, and life in total darkness
paragraphs: Endurance22's cameras also captured the ship's wheel, still standing at her stern. No sunlight reaches 3,008 m, so nothing here photosynthesises; instead the hull has become a deep-sea oasis of filter feeders that strain edible particles from the passing water.

Marine biologists reviewing the footage identified sea stars (including brisingid sea stars), glass sponges, sea squirts, a bright yellow stalked sea lily (a crinoid), and a large white anemone near the wheel. They also spotted a ghostly white squat lobster, likely of the genus Munidopsis -- the first record of that kind of animal in this part of the Weddell Sea. "The ship is cool," said British Antarctic Survey marine biogeographer Huw Griffiths, "but look at those things living on it."

entries.title: Masts down, funnel toppled
paragraphs: Although the hull is remarkably sound, Endurance did not come through entirely undamaged. FMHT's survey found her masts down and her funnel toppled, with the heaviest damage concentrated around the poop deck at the stern and the waist amidships. Photographs of the wreck suggest she struck the seabed bow- or keel-first as she went down.
The damage is consistent with how she sank: crushed by pack ice over months, then going down stern-first as recorded by witnesses in 1915, after a fall of 3 km through freezing water.
Look forward of the hull for the fallen-rigging scan marker.

facts.label: Sank
facts.value: 21 November 1915, after ~10 months beset in pack ice

entries.title: Worsley's position, and the search that found her
paragraphs: Captain Frank Worsley, Endurance's navigator, logged the ship's sinking position from the ice as 68°39′30″S 52°26′30″W. A 2022 peer-reviewed study of his navigation log (Squire & Bell, Journal of Navigation) found the fix itself was sound work under brutal conditions, but flagged real sources of uncertainty: few navigational sights were possible around the time of the sinking, and chronometer error accumulates the longer it goes unchecked at sea. The authors estimate the combined uncertainty at several nautical miles in both latitude and longitude.

The Endurance22 team used Worsley's position, adjusted for that uncertainty, to define their search box and found the wreck within it. UKAHT describes the wreck as roughly four miles (6.4 km) south of his recorded position. Measuring between the published log and wreck coordinates gives about 10 km to the south-south-east.
This scan marks seabed at Worsley's logged position. His navigation, and 107 years of searching, finally led back to the ship.

entries.title: A very flat piece of ocean floor
paragraphs: Away from the wreck, this part of the Weddell Sea floor is remarkably featureless: across the whole ~70 x 33 km tile the terrain ranges only from about 2,915 m to 3,096 m, a relief of under 200 m. Two kilometres west of the wreck the seabed is about 2,988 m deep, a gentle 12 m rise from the 3,000 m reading at the wreck itself.
The deep Weddell Sea plain lies far from ridges and canyons. The coarser GEBCO-derived grid used here also smooths seabed features smaller than a few kilometres.

entries.title: A protected monument, not a grave
paragraphs: Every man aboard Endurance survived her sinking; Shackleton had already led the crew off onto the ice before she went down. So unlike Titanic or Bismarck, this wreck is not a war grave or a gravesite -- but she is still one of the best-preserved and most significant wrecks in the world, and international law protects her accordingly.

The Antarctic Treaty System designated the (then still unfound) wreck a Historic Site and Monument, HSM No. 93, in 2019 -- three years before anyone located her. That status makes it an offence to touch, disturb, or remove anything from the site; Endurance22's own survey and filming work had to be carried out without any contact with the wreck.

Since the discovery, the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust and Historic England have led a Conservation Management Plan for the site, and have proposed expanding the protection zone from its original 500 m radius to 1,500 m to cover the full debris field, with a longer-term goal of a formal Antarctic Specially Protected Area designation. Warming Antarctic waters and increasing ship traffic in the region are cited as growing risks.
Survey the wreck through photographs and scans, leaving its timber, fittings and surrounding debris undisturbed.
